rules.title: Just cause required to evict tenants in units covered by the Rent Ordinance
rules.requirement: In San Francisco, a landlord can evict you from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for one of 17 listed just cause reasons, and that reason must be the landlord's dominant motive; a lease simply expiring or a change in ownership is not a just cause. This also applies to many units exempt from rent increase limits, including units first certified for occupancy after June 13, 1979.

coverage.summary: Rental units covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance, including some units exempt from its rent increase limits (newly constructed units with a first Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, Costa-Hawkins exempt tenancies, and some tenancies whose rent is regulated by another government agency).
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Units not covered by the Rent Ordinance (exemptions not detailed on this page)

rules.exemptions: Page does not detail which units fall outside Rent Ordinance coverage. Eviction protections extend to some units exempt from rent increase limits.
rules.penalty: A landlord who evicts or tries to evict a tenant unlawfully may be subject to substantial civil and/or criminal liability.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction. Note that the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute "just cause" for eviction.
rules.interaction: Tenancies eligible for rent increases under the state Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act remain subject to the city's just cause eviction provisions. Ellis Act withdrawal is a listed just cause.

notes: Official Rent Board summary of S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9(a). The page does not specify the exact coverage exemptions of the Rent Ordinance, notice periods, or relocation assistance, so those are left out. The 1979 Certificate of Occupancy date describes units exempt from rent limits but still covered by just cause, so it is not used as a coverage cutoff.
